title: Why Huldah Was Chosen Instead of Jeremiah
paragraphs: Why Huldah Was Chosen Instead of Jeremiah
The room was full of men.
Priests were there.
Scribes were there.
Officials were there.
The king's representatives were there.
And somewhere in Jerusalem, one of the greatest prophets who ever lived was there too.
Jeremiah.
Yet when the lost Book of the Law was discovered in the days of King Josiah, the delegation sent by the king did not go to Jeremiah.
They went to Huldah.
For many readers of Scripture, that detail passes by unnoticed.
But when you slow down and sit with the text, the question emerges almost immediately:
Why Huldah?
Why would God choose a woman prophet in that moment when Jeremiah was already ministering in Judah?
Why would kings, priests, and national leaders seek her counsel?
And what does that choice reveal about the heart of God?
The answer takes us into one of the most beautiful realities in Scripture.
God has never been impressed by human status.
He has always been looking for faithful hearts.
The discovery that changed everything
The story unfolds in 2 Kings 22 and 2 Chronicles 34.
During repairs to the Temple, Hilkiah the high priest discovered what appears to have been the Book of the Law.
When the words were read before King Josiah, something devastating happened.
The king tore his clothes.
He realized Judah had abandoned the covenant.
Generations had drifted from God.
Judgment was coming.
The king's response reveals a heart that still trembled before the Word of God.
Instead of making excuses, Josiah sought divine counsel.
The text says:
"Go, inquire of the LORD for me, and for the people, and for all Judah."
That inquiry led directly to Huldah.
Not Jeremiah.
Not Zephaniah.
Huldah.
The woman many modern believers know almost nothing about.
Yet heaven knew exactly who she was.
The Hebrew text reveals something powerful
The Bible calls her "Huldah the prophetess."
The Hebrew phrase is:
"Nevi'ah" (נְבִיאָה)
The feminine form of prophet.
Not prophet's wife.
Not assistant prophet.
Not honorary prophet.
Not someone occasionally inspired.
A prophet.
A genuine spokesperson entrusted by God with His words.
The same God who called Moses.
The same God who called Isaiah.
The same God who called Jeremiah.
The same God spoke through Huldah.
Scripture never apologizes for her authority.
Neither should we.
The delegation came because they believed God was speaking through her.
And they were right.
The scandal nobody expected
There is a subtle scandal hidden in this story.
Ancient societies were overwhelmingly patriarchal.
Positions of influence were usually held by men.
Yet when a national crisis erupted, God placed His authoritative voice in the mouth of a woman.
This is not an attack on men.
It is a revelation about God.
The Lord has never operated according to human hierarchies.
Throughout Scripture He repeatedly chooses the unexpected.
The youngest son over the oldest.
The shepherd over the king.
The tax collector over the religious elite.
The fisherman over the scholar.
The crucified Messiah over the conquering warrior.
Again and again, God overturns human expectations.
Because God does not evaluate people the way people evaluate people.
As the Lord told Samuel:
"Man looks on the outward appearance, but the LORD looks on the heart."
The issue was never gender.
The issue was faithfulness.
Jeremiah was not being rejected
Many assume that choosing Huldah somehow diminished Jeremiah.
Nothing in Scripture suggests this.
Jeremiah remained one of God's greatest prophets.
His ministry stretched across decades.
He faithfully proclaimed truth through immense suffering.
The issue is not Jeremiah versus Huldah.
The issue is understanding God's sovereignty.
The Lord raises different servants for different assignments.
Sometimes God uses Elijah.
Sometimes Elisha.
Sometimes Deborah.
Sometimes Isaiah.
Sometimes Mary.
Sometimes Peter.
Sometimes Paul.
And sometimes Huldah.
The kingdom of God is not a competition.
It is an orchestra.
Different instruments.
One Composer.
Different voices.
One message.
Different callings.
One Lord.
What Huldah understood that the nation missed
When the officials arrived, Huldah immediately confirmed the coming judgment.
She did not soften God's message.
She did not dilute the truth.
She did not tell the king what he wanted to hear.
She declared exactly what God had spoken.
That kind of courage is rare.
Especially when national leaders are standing in front of you.
Especially when your message will not be popular.
Especially when judgment is the topic.
But Huldah feared God more than she feared people.
That is what made her trustworthy.
The Hebrew Scriptures consistently present prophets as covenant prosecutors.
They reminded Israel that God's promises and warnings were both real.
Huldah understood that.
She refused to exchange truth for comfort.
Yet her message contained something astonishing.
Grace.
Always grace.
Because God never speaks judgment without revealing His heart.
The king who tore his clothes
Huldah delivered devastating news.
Judgment would come.
The nation's rebellion had consequences.
But then she spoke directly about Josiah.
The Lord said:
"Because your heart was responsive and you humbled yourself before the LORD..."
Those words changed everything.
Judgment would still come eventually.
But Josiah would be gathered to his fathers in peace.
Why?
Because repentance matters.
Humility matters.
Brokenness matters.
The Hebrew concept behind humility carries the idea of being brought low before God.
Not destroyed.
Not humiliated.
But surrendered.
Josiah's tears mattered to heaven.
His repentance mattered to heaven.
His trembling mattered to heaven.
And that points us directly to Jesus Christ.
From Huldah to Christ
The entire Bible ultimately leads to Jesus.
Even this story.
Especially this story.
Because Huldah's message exposes humanity's deepest problem.
Sin is real.
Judgment is real.
Rebellion has consequences.
But God's mercy is also real.
That tension reaches its fulfillment at the cross.
In Greek, one of the New Testament's most beautiful words is:
"Charis" (χάρις)
Grace.
Unmerited favor.
Undeserved kindness.
The scandalous generosity of God toward sinners.
At Calvary, justice and mercy met.
Judgment was not ignored.
It was satisfied.
The wrath deserved by sinners was absorbed by Christ.
The punishment fell upon Him.
The grace flowed toward us.
That is why every story of repentance in Scripture whispers the Gospel.
Every torn garment points toward the torn body of Christ.
Every cry for mercy points toward the cross.
Every act of surrender points toward the Savior.
The forgotten prophetess who still speaks
Huldah appears briefly in Scripture.
Only a handful of verses.
No lengthy book bears her name.
No extended narrative follows her ministry.
Yet her influence helped shape one of the greatest revivals in Judah's history.
Never underestimate what God can do through a faithful life.
The world measures importance by visibility.
God measures importance by faithfulness.
Many believers spend their lives waiting for a platform.
God is looking for obedience.
Many want recognition.
God desires surrender.
Many want influence.
God seeks faithfulness.
Huldah reminds us that heaven's measurements are radically different from earth's measurements.
The same truth still confronts us today.
God is not searching for the most famous person.
He is searching for the most faithful person.
The invitation hidden inside the story
Perhaps the deepest question is not why Huldah was chosen instead of Jeremiah.
Perhaps the deeper question is this:
If God needed someone trustworthy today, could He trust us?
Could He trust us with truth?
Could He trust us with influence?
Could He trust us with suffering?
Could He trust us with obscurity?
Could He trust us with His Word?
Huldah's story is not ultimately about a woman replacing a man.
It is about a God who chooses faithful servants.
And that truth changes everything.
Because every believer who has ever felt overlooked, forgotten, insignificant, dismissed, or unseen can find hope here.
The God who saw Huldah sees you.
The God who spoke through Huldah still speaks through surrendered lives.
The God who honored faithfulness still honors faithfulness.
And the God who sent His Son to save sinners is still rewriting stories today.
Maybe that is why this account continues to resonate thousands of years later.
Not because of Huldah alone.
But because her story reveals the heart of Jesus.
The Savior who specializes in choosing the unexpected.
The Redeemer who turns obscurity into purpose.
The King who transforms failures into testimonies.
The Lord who takes broken lives and writes redemption across every page.
Have you ever felt unseen while waiting for God to use you?
Supporting this ministry helps biblical content like this reach more hearts, equip more believers, and glorify Christ through truth-centered discipleship.
One day we will discover that heaven remembered every act of faithfulness the world never noticed.
